title: From Perception to Programs: Learning to Reconstruct the Visual World
description: From Perception to Programs: Learning to Reconstruct the Visual World Abstract: Modern AI systems have demonstrated remarkable abilities to recognize and generate visual patterns. Yet many problems, from scientific discovery to engineering design, require more than modeling observations: they require inferring the processes that generate them. Can machines discover the reusable operations and abstractions needed to reconstruct the world from limited evidence?I will explore this question through origami, a domain where complex structures emerge from sequences of simple folds. I will present OrigamiBench, which reveals limitations in the ability of vision-language models to reason about geometric transformations and compose them into executable folding programs. These findings motivate the development of representations and abstractions that support compositional reasoning.I will discuss my work on reliable self-supervised representation learning, showing how principled inductive biases can prevent representational collapse, and on neuro-symbolic learning, showing how neural representations can be integrated with symbolic knowledge to improve generalization from limited data. Building on these foundations, I will introduce unsupervised neural induction, a research direction aimed at jointly learning neural representations and a richer language of reusable abstractions from visual observations, moving beyond programs expressed in a predefined language. The long-term goal is to enable machines to develop interpretable, executable models of the visual world that can be tested, composed, and refined through experience. Bio: Emanuele Sansone is a Marie Skłodowska-Curie Global Postdoctoral Fellow at KU Leuven and a former researcher at MIT CSAIL. His research lies at the intersection of unsupervised learning, neuro-symbolic AI, and program synthesis. He received his PhD from the University of Trento and has led international research collaborations supported by European and US research programs. title: CSAIL FORUM with Daniel Jackson: The Key to Agentic Software Development
description: CSAIL FORUM with Daniel Jackson: The Key to Agentic Software Development Abstract: AI-driven coding agents have opened a new world for building software. But applied in standard ways they are likely to just create a mountain of technical and cognitive debt. How do you take control and produce reliable and maintainable software? This talk, directed both at those who build software and those who are accountable for it, will explain how.Bio:Daniel Jackson is professor of computer science at MIT, and associate director of CSAIL. For his research in software, he won the ACM SIGSOFT Impact Award, the ACM SIGSOFT Outstanding Research Award and was made an ACM Fellow.He is the lead designer of the Alloy modeling language, and author of Software Abstractions. He chaired a National Academies study on software dependability, and has collaborated on software projects with NASA on air-traffic control, with Massachusetts General Hospital on proton therapy, and with Toyota on autonomous cars.His most recent book, Essence of Software, offers a fresh approach to software design, and shows how thinking about software in terms of concepts and their relationships can lead to more usable and effective software.
